original_question: Does there exist a connected signed graph Γ = (G, σ) whose underlying graph G is not complete, whose adjacency spectrum is symmetric with respect to the origin, but which is not sign-symmetric, meaning Γ is not switching isomorphic to its negation -Γ = (G, -σ)?
target_in_paper: Section 3.1, Problem 3.3: "Are there non-complete connected signed graphs whose spectrum is symmetric with respect to the origin but they are not sign-symmetric?"
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper’s intended target extremely closely. It correctly asks an existence question, keeps the connected and non-complete restrictions, uses the intended spectral symmetry condition, and correctly unpacks "not sign-symmetric" as not being switching isomorphic to the negated signature.
missing_details: In this paper, the relevant spectrum is the adjacency spectrum of the signed adjacency matrix A(Γ); the paper often says simply "spectrum" because Section 1 sets adjacency matrices as the default throughout.
To be fully stand-alone, "symmetric with respect to the origin" should be understood as multiset symmetry of the eigenvalues of A(Γ): if λ occurs, then -λ occurs with the same multiplicity.
The paper’s notion of sign-symmetric uses switching isomorphism, not merely switching equivalence; that allows switching together with a vertex permutation.
The negated signed graph -Γ means (G, -σ), i.e. the same underlying graph with every edge sign reversed.
refined_question: Does there exist a connected signed graph Γ = (G, σ), with non-complete underlying graph G, such that the adjacency spectrum of Γ is symmetric with respect to 0, but Γ is not sign-symmetric; equivalently, Γ is not switching isomorphic to its negation -Γ = (G, -σ)?
justification: The draft is essentially a paper-faithful restatement of Problem 3.3. Section 3.1 first introduces sign-symmetric signed graphs by the condition Γ is switching isomorphic to -Γ, then states in Theorem 3.2 that every sign-symmetric signed graph has spectrum symmetric about the origin. The authors immediately explain that the converse fails for signed complete graphs via Seidel-matrix examples, and then ask precisely whether such counterexamples also exist among non-complete connected signed graphs. So the closest official target is Problem 3.3, not a broader neighboring question.
